title: Shelf lease smoothing and tempered surge handshake - PRD notes
content:
Problem statement:

We see two recurring operator/customer failure modes for Dedicated capacity during unpredictable spikes: (1) noisy tenants cause sudden headroom exhaustion leading to preemptions and SLA violations for other tenants; (2) aggressive failover to lower-fidelity model variants causes poor user experience without a clear contract or predictable cost. Current designs (hard quotas, burst credits, preemption) are brittle: they either punish tenants too quickly or allow noisy spikes to cascade.

Goal (product):
- Provide a predictable, auditable mechanism that absorbs short bursts with a controlled impact on cost and latency, while preserving tenant isolation and clear SLAs.
- Offer tenants an opt-in contract that trades graded fidelity (timely partial responses / low-cost model variants) for reduced eviction risk during spikes.
- Reduce operator toil for incident recovery by automating a deterministic staggered recovery process and explicit attestation for fidelity tradeoffs.

High-level solution summary:
Introduce two coupled concepts: Shelf Leases and the Tempered Surge Handshake.

1) Shelf Leases:
- Short-duration, fast-provisioning capacity slices ("shelves") carved out of a dedicated pool. Shelves are transient: 15s–10min reservations automatically managed by the control plane.
- Shelves are fundable in two modes: buffered (pre-allocated from a tenant’s reserved pool) and opportunistic (borrowed from a shared recovery reservoir with payback semantics).
- Each shelf is accompanied by a small attestation token describing the contract: fidelity constraints (which model classes are acceptable), max latency degradation, and a refund/credit profile.

2) Tempered Surge Handshake (TSH):
- A 3-step negotiation between tenant agent, scheduler, and recovery broker when a spike arrives and no immediate dedicated capacity is available.
- Phase A (Offer): scheduler signals possible shelf(s) with an attestation contract (token).
- Phase B (Bid): tenant's serving layer decides to accept a contract (e.g., allow 10% quality degradation or fall back to 4-bit quantized variant) or decline. Decision may be automatic for tenants that pre-authorize a fidelity profile.
- Phase C (Activate): If accepted, the shelf is provisioned and traffic routed; metrics and a short-term billing ledger entry created. If declined, standard fallback path applies (rate-limited queueing, preemption).

Why different from existing approaches:
- Instead of opaque burst credits or blunt preemptions, shelf leases make the tradeoff explicit (attestation token) and auditable.
- Tenants can pre-declare fidelity profiles and opt-in for automatic TSH acceptance reducing tail latency spikes without surprise evictions.
- Operators get deterministic recovery/decay behavior (see runbook) reducing incident cycles.

User stories:
- As an SRE for a SaaS customer, I want my high-priority routes to avoid eviction during short bursts at the cost of a pre-declared 5% model fidelity drop, so downstream UX stays acceptable.
- As a Redwood product owner, I want tenants to be able to buy opportunistic shelves when they exceed reserved headroom, with transparent temporary billing and an automated payback schedule.
- As an operator, I want an automated staggered recovery for drained pools to avoid cascading hot restarts.

Requirements (measurable):
- P1: 90% of spikes < 60s must be absorbed by either reserved shelves or opportunistic shelves when tenant has pre-authorized a fidelity profile.
- P2: The attestation token must contain machine-readable fidelity constraints and be logged for audit; token issuance latency <= 50ms.
- P3: Billing ledger entry created within 100ms of shelf activation; visible in Console under per-route cost.
- P4: No increase in 99th percentile latency for other tenants in the same pool by >5% due to shelf activations (isolation guardrails).

Design details:
- Shelf sizing: small fixed quanta (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 1 GPU-equivalent slot) to limit blast radius.
- Decay model: opportunistic shelves carry a time-decay credit that requires payback via reduced capacity allocation over next N minutes or via billing reconciliation.
- Isolation fences: when a shelf activates, the scheduler increases CPU/GPU isolation at the node-level via cgroup QoS settings and enforces kernel-level throttles for background processes.
- Fidelity profiles: JSON schema describing which model variants are acceptable, allowed quantization levels, max acceptable increase in hallucination risk (heuristic), and minimum token-level output constraints.

Operational runbook (high level):
- Detection: spike triggers shelf offer if reserved headroom < threshold.
- Automation: if tenant has "auto-accept" fidelity, TSH proceeds without human intervention.
- Escalation: if opportunistic reservoir fill rate > X% and recovery payback backlog > Y minutes, trigger operator alert and reject new opportunistic shelves.
- Recovery stagger: when a pool drains below safe capacity, we gracefully pause new shelf offers, stagger decommissions in 30s windows, and proactively migrate long-running KV caches to warm standby nodes.

Telemetry & metrics to collect:
- per-tenant shelf activations / minute (time series)
- attestation token accept/reject ratio (per route)
- mean token issuance latency, shelf provisioning latency
- opportunistic reservoir utilization and payback backlog minutes
- downstream quality regressions (prompt/eval based) correlated with shelf activations

Console UX / APIs:
- New fields in Dedicated plan UI: "Fidelity opt-in profile", daily opportunistic shelf spend cap, preferred shelf decay policy.
- API: POST /v1/dedicated/shelves/offer to request preliminary attestation (returns token + cost estimate).
- Webhook: shelf_activation events with token and billing_id for immediate routing and observability.

Rollout plan (canary -> GA):
1) Internal-only test with synthetic noisy tenants; exercise TSH and recovery staggering (2 weeks).
2) Invite-only early adopter customers (3–5 tenants) with explicit SLA docs and billing sandbox (4 weeks).
3) Wider beta with telemetry-driven thresholds enabled (6 weeks).
4) GA behind an account-level opt-in; defaults off.

Billing model (sketch):
- Opportunistic shelf usage billed at a premium multiplier (e.g., 1.5x) with an optional payback schedule that spreads cost over following billing cycles when pre-authorized.
- Reserved-buffer shelves draw from committed capacity and are billed against existing reserved utilization.

Open questions / tech risks (to resolve in next iteration):
- How to quantify "fidelity degradation" across different model families reliably? Need an eval harness to measure regressions tied to shelf activations. (Linked: CONFLUENCE-6453)
- Edge-case: two cooperating tenants both opt into auto-accept and simultaneously claim multiple shelves — need stronger global arbitration to avoid oversubscription of node-level nic/cpu resources.
- Security: attestation tokens must be cryptographically verifiable and short-lived; which KMS flow do we use?

Notes to self / implementation hints:
- Prototype attestation schema in a single YAML file and wire a cheap token signer. Implement token in scheduler middleware before spending significant infra changes.
- Simulation: adapt the existing capacity simulator (JIRA-DEDI-1127) to add shelf quanta and payback scheduling.
- Quick experiment: enable opportunistic shelves as a feature flag on a single pool and route traffic with canned fuzzed spikes.

Appendix (short sketches):
- Attestation example (text): {"fidelity_profile": "fallback-to-llama-4bit", "max_latency_increase_ms": 150, "duration_sec": 120, "billing_token": "shelf-20241105-abc"}
- Handshake pseudocode (very rough):
  offer = scheduler.offer_shelf(tenant, route)
  if tenant.auto_accept(profile_matches(offer)):
    scheduler.activate(offer)
  else:
    notify(tenant) -> await accept/decline (50ms timeout)

Next steps (actionable):
- Align on attestation schema (owner: Priya; due: 2024-11-12).
- Build small prototype of token issuance (owner: Rafael; due: 2024-11-22).
- Run first pool-level canary and collect payback backlog metrics (owner: Ayesha; due: 2024-12-06).

-- end --
